chunks.text: Working to a different rhythm With CBC Newsworld's first anniversary just around the corner-the birthday party is on Monday, July 31 - Joan Donaldson, Donaldson, head of the network, is "incredibly glad our first year is over." Even before Newsworld went on the air, the doom and gloom merchants merchants predicted failure or, worse, irrelevance. After all, said the begrudgers, how could a Canadian all-news service compete with Ted Turner's giant American operation at CNN. However galling, it is probably inevitable that Canadian developments will be compared with American counterparts. Even when the comparison is useless (like apples and oranges), the Canadians almost always appear the losers because the standard measures are quantitative: money, numbers, bigness. By all those standards, CBC Newsworld is a small operation - a compact model. A staff of around 200 people, working from four studios, produce Canada's only 24-hour 24-hour news service. What makes Newsworld distinctive, distinctive, if not truly amazing, in Canadian Canadian broadcasting is the production of cross-country programming - all day long, seven days a week-which does not originate in Toronto. Toronto. The Newsworld day begins in Halifax, where the operation runs out of a couple of trailers hitched up to the CBC building, and then switches to Calgary. Ottawa is the centre for weekend programming. Toronto's role is to coordinate satellite satellite feeds and slot in the advertising advertising breaks. The importance of this decision, as Donaldson stresses, is to shift the all-important "gatekeepers", the filters who organize our per ception of the news, away from the traditional central Canadian focus. Before Newsworld, the Hughes inquiry into child abuse at Mount Cashel or the Manitoba Aboriginal Justice inquiry would have been "provincial" stories deserving, at best, a two-minute summary on The National. On Newsworld, both were covered live for extended periods. Donaldson explains that the choice to provide extensive live coverage of events like these was a conscious one: "Newsworld works to a different rhythm, providing live coverage to set events in context context and without the usual talking heads providing commentary." One explanation for Donaldson's vision - "I prefer a 12 minute interview to a three minute one, and particularly to the 30-second sound bite." - is her previous experience experience in CBC Radio, which has always had a more leisurely and more considered notion of how to tell its stories. With a limited - and closely watched - budget, and licensing restrictions laid down by the CRTC, Newsworld operates on a shoestring in a very expensive milieu. The one drawback in the license definition of the network as providing only information, no matter how broadly defined, over the full 24 hours, is the temptation to fill space with boring round-table round-table discussions in dull sets. On the plus side, Newsworld has the benefit of being able to draw much of its material from the full complement of CBC's regular correspondents correspondents both here in Canada and in the rest of the world. This principle, principle, incorporated in the United Nations Charter, says that no country can change existing borders or overthrow somebody else's government by force and that the results of such an aggression will not be recognized. This principle is very important if our future is not to be as full of wars as our past, and it is actually quite widely observed. chunks.text: ROBERT FULFORD SPECIAL TO THE GAZETTE Ninety years old in 1957, the great American architect Frank Lloyd Wright was summoned by the government of Iraq to design a series of buildings in Baghdad, beginning with an opera house in a new culture centre. . Wright had loved The Arabian Nights since childhood, and the idea of working within an exotic and half-understood culture made him wildly excited. In Iraq he studied collections of Su-merian Su-merian art, and decided that ancient Sumer would inspire him, just as traditional traditional Japanese art had sharpened his imagination when he built one of his masterpieces, the Imperial Hotel in Tokyo, Tokyo, in 1921. Back home in the U.S. he was full of the optimism that continually surprised and refreshed everyone near him. "When this commission came from Baghdad, I was astonished, delighted and puzzled. I didn't know how they got a renegade like me, a rebel, but they did ' . . . we've got a great opportunity." Vigorous, adventurous Soon he had a sheaf of drawings an opera house, a museum, a park, a plan for a city centre, even a monument to the caliph Haroun-al Rashid. These Baghdad proposals fill eight wonderful pages in Frank Lloyd Wright Drawings, edited by Bruce Brooks Pfeiffer. They're deliriously imaginative, strikingly strikingly Arabic in tone, and yet marked clearly by Wright's own style and spirit. They remind us again how vigorous and adventurous he was even in his last years (he died in 1959). But they also produce in the reader reader of this book perhaps the loveliest loveliest of all the books devoted to Wright a certain melancholy. Because, of course, there are no Wright buildings in Baghdad, and there never were. A change of government killed all the plans, so each of these drawings carries beneath it in the book the dreaded word "(PROJECT)," meaning it was not built. That word appears again and again under the drawings Pfeiffer has chosen, so that after a while the book acquires a ghostly character. What it shows us is a whole city of ideas that never became buildings. There are churches, hotels, cinemas, libraries libraries (including a Carnegie Library proposed for Pembroke, Ont.), houses, " -7- ml $ : - H forthrightly Another of Wright's aborted works: store project for Ahmedebad, India, in 1946. office buildings all existing only as handsome, ghostly images on the page. Every architect lives part of his career in frustration over stillborn projects. But when we consider that Wright was the greatest of all American architects,- the list of aborted plans seems remarkably remarkably long. One reason for it was his personality. He took an almost god-like view of himself, himself, and this produced an arrogance that could make life hell for clients. The other reason, more important, was his approach to architecture. "He was visibly exhausted and the owner of the boat just picked him up with his hands and put him in a plastic can until we arrived," McCann said. Louis McCann, director of wild- McCann said the baby seal will stay in his new, temporary home an outdoor cage with a basin of water until he gets a clean bill of health from the veterinarian. "We ran blood tests and if all goes well, he'll be released in the Ta-doussac Ta-doussac area on Tuesday," McCann said. Junior began to eat some fish yesterday yesterday afternoon but, according to McCann, "did an awful lot of snoozing throughout the day." SPCA workers put the seal on a diet of frozen smelt, supplemented by sea capsules and salt pills to keep his sodium levels up. McCann said it's rare to find seals, who normally live in salt water, in the Montreal area. "We gained experience with seals in 1987 when one was rescued in the La Ronde marina," he said. No such animal, you say. Wrong, Philistine. In fact, Rotten Reviews I was such a dare I say critical critical and commercial hit that it actually actually spawned a sequel, Rotten Reviews Reviews II (Penguin). How's that for bittersweet irony? The first volume contained negative negative reviews of works published up to the year 1960. But since there was such a wealth of material, an update seemed essential; and for fun-seeking sadists writers or non-writers No. 2 lives up to the original. It's a laugh-riot, to be cherished in a small, enclosed and, preferably, plumbing-equipped room of your home. Bill Henderson, an occasional novelist and editor of the two volumes, volumes, is astounded by the success of the first book. He is even more astounded that authors like Margaret Margaret Atwood, Allen Ginsberg, Erica Erica Jong and Joyce Carol Oates, among many others, actually contributed contributed to the second volume by passing along nasty, mean-spirited mentions of their works. Sense of humor If there were ever any doubt, this proves that prima-donna authors do have a sense of humor. Whether they have any respect for the critic is another issue entirely. While critics often proclaim their rotten reviews are aimed only to strengthen the art form and make authors better humans, this view is not often shared by the writer. Way back when, the legendary Percy Bysshe Shelley (1792-1822) noted that: "Contemporary criticism criticism only represents the amount of ignorance genius has to contend with . . . and time will reverse the judgment of the vulgar." Andre Bourbeau, the provincial manpower manpower and income security minister, sent $11,000 worth of gold and silver pins to his 2,600 welfare agents as a token of appreciation for their hard work during the past year. Since last August, employees at 127 welfare offices across Quebec have been busy converting dossiers of recipients into 144 different pay scales to conform with the government's welfare reform law, Bill 37. "This was a very inappropriate time for them to give us these things," said Jean Robert, a spokesman for the union representing the welfare agents. "It's more of an insult than a sign of gratitude because because we have already denounced this reform." On Wednesday, more than 82,000 of Quebec's 570,000 welfare recipients will have their cheques slashed by as much as $ 100. And some food-bank operators fear they won't be able to cope with the increasing demand for emergency emergency food from recipients with less money to spend on groceries. They're not alone in their concern. The welfare office in the Quebec City suburb of Li-moilou Li-moilou has hired a security guard because managers fear possible violence from angry recipients. The government is offering stress-management courses for its civil servants. The $2.2-billion reform package, introduced in May of last year by Bourbeau, contains three programs: work and employment incentives, financial support and parental wage assistance. Zsa Zsa Gabor checked into the city jail yesterday yesterday to begin serving a three-day sentence for slapping a Beverly Hills motorcycle police officer. The 72-year-old celebrity, dressed in slacks and a sweatshirt and clutching a "good-luck frog,' appeared in good spirits when she checked in at I p.m., said Fern Ruiz, a police department records clerk. After a three-week, highly publicized publicized trial, Gabor was convicted of three misdemeanors Sept. 29 arising arising from her June 14, 1989, run-in with Officer Paul Kramer. Kramer, who stopped Gabor's Rolls-Royce because its license plates had expired, testified that Gabor drove away from him. When he pulled her over again, she swore and slapped his face. The actress, who unsuccessfully appealed the 72-hour jail sentence, is to be released Monday. Ruiz said Gabor was the only prisoner at the 17-pcrson jail in this Los Angeles suburb when she checked in, but that others were expected expected yesterday. CITRUS The marriage of California and French cuisine in this trendy St. Laurent Blvd. establishment is a marriage made in heaven if ever there was one. Talented young Norman Laprise presents an exquisite menu and makes imaginative use of fruits, vegetables and fresh herbs in most of his light sauces. Everything is fresh the place doesn't even own a freezer. Recently sampled starters included a heavenly ravioli-like package of thinly sliced salmon filled with chopped snails and spinach in a sauce of pureed asparagus, cream and ginger. Another, lasagna, actually contained one thin layer of pasta to separate the thicker layers of smoked salmon, leaf spinach and goat cheese. Grilled medallions of Barbary duck perfumed with clover honey and cloves and nuggets of lamb leg with a coulis of fresh basil were outstanding main dishes. Vegetables are superb the deep-fried beet chips may put french fries out of the market. Sweets are-also great. Everything is table d'hote with the first two courses included in the price of the third main course which ranges from $27.95 to $33.95. Open nightly from 6 p.m. to 11 p.m. Licensed. chunks.text: FES KASBAT This very pretty Moroccan restaurant has low sofas and tables in semi-private "booths" along its sides and standard tables in the middle. It offers a much wider range of Moroccan cuisine than its simpler cousins, the ubiquitous couscous houses. Try any of the excellent briks or chef's fingers for starters. The place does feature a wide range of couscous dishes, of course, well made but timidly seasoned. A better bet are its tajines (stews cooked in earthenware casseroles), although the one sampled chicken with olives and rice was barely saved from terminal blandness by the wonderful Moroccan pickled lemon slices. A small dash of fiery harissa can correct this timidity in a hurry, but a word in the ear of the waitress when ordering might be more productive. There is also a good selection of brochettes and grills, and there are good oriental pastries for dessert and a belly dancer most evenings. Main dishes in the $10-to-$14 range. Open daily except Mon. from 11 a.m. to I a.m. Licensed. China finds scapegoat for protest ROBERT BENJAMIN BALTIMORE SUN BEIJING China's divided leadership finally has settled on a political scapegoat for the 1989 Tiananmen Square protests: the chief aide of ousted Communist Party chief Zhao Ziyang. v: The longtime aide, Bao Tong, 59, is expected to be put on trial in secret secret today on charges of leaking state secrets and inciting counterrevolutionary counterrevolutionary propaganda, according according to statements by his relatives to foreign reporters. The closed-door trial represents a compromise solution to a long-stalled long-stalled effort by the party to close the books on the massivepro-democracy demonstrations that were brutally crushed by the Chinese army June 3-4, 1989. The proceeding is China's most important political trial since the 1980 senlencings of the Gang of Four Mao Tse-tung's widow, Jiang Qiang, and three other ultra-leftists ultra-leftists who were held responsible responsible for leading the disastrous Cultural Cultural Revolution in the 1960s and 1970s. China has rejected requests by the United States and other foreign governments that independent observers observers be allowed to witness Bao's trial. Even his family will not be allowed allowed to attend. It is virtually certain that the trial will find Bao guilty. But the severity of his sentence, which could be more than 10 years, may provide some insight as to the current status of the power struggle between party leftists and reformers. Political divisions within the party have rendered it unable to put on trial Zhao, who has been under house arrest in Beijing since losing the party's top post as a result of the Tiananmen protests. However, trying Bao has emerged as a way to attack the former party chiefs moderately reformist political political policies as the main source of the protests. Bao has been imprisoned since May 1989 China analysts believe that Bao is being tried now in an effort to lay to rest the Tiananmen affair before the opening of a key party congress this fall, a meeting that could result in top-level leadership shifts. Bao's trial is also a clear sign that "the party congress will only be about economic reform and definitely definitely not about political reforms or any initiatives in the field of justice," justice," a European diplomat said. "There's not going to be any political political liberalization." Perot exited his undeclared presidential campaign Thursday as suddenly and surprisingly as he entered it almost five months ago. Three characteristics were made apparent by his experience: experience: he lacked the patience to tough it out or compromise in adversarial situations; he was unwilling unwilling to delegate authority; and not even his fresh look and can-do attitude could break through the two-party system. "Ross Perot, with his top-down, hands-on crisis management style is probably just as well as a captain of industry rather than moving over into the political world, where I think different attributes and skills may get you further," said Representative Vic Fazio, a California Democrat. The topsy-turvy political world of 1992 had seemed eager to accept what many perceived as Perot's unique attributes for the nation's highest office. "I think Perot has reinvented American politics," said William Gormley, a Georgetown University professor professor of government. "It remains to be seen if someone someone else will take advantage of the new ground rules." Frustrated by governmental gridlock in Washington and a stagnant economy, primary voters stunned pundits pundits and establishment politicians by giving impressive levels of support to mavericks such as Republican Pat Buchanan and Democrat Jerry Brown, while turning incumbents out of office in unprecedented numbers. Perot made his conditional entry into the campaign spontaneously in February during an appearance on the Larry King Live show on CNN and, as he became fond of pointing out, immediately turned the presidential presidential race on its head. If volunteers could get his name on the ballot in all 50 states, Perot said, he would agree to run and gladly be their "servant" if elected. Impressed by the Texan's straightforward style, his fabled business acumen and acts of patriotism, Americans Americans responded and Perot shot into contention in presidential presidential preference polls. As of last week, Perot nominating nominating petitions had been filed in 33 states and he was certified to appear on the ballot in 24. But a spate of setbacks, including the resignation of campaign co-manager Ed Rollins last Wednesday, culminated culminated in Perot's withdrawal. Rollins complained that Perot wouldn't listen to advice and refused to formally declare a Perot for the People candidacy or take other necessary steps to remain a viable candidate. candidate."Ross Perot is a businessman. He's used to making his own decisions," said John Jay Hooker, a Tennessee businessman who helped persuade Perot to run. "His instincts were not to surround himself with a lot of political handlers, and when he did, he found it hard to work in that environment." Perot said he quit because he calculated that he couldn't win and didn't want to throw the election into the I louse of Representatives. The forgotten The Innu take on Ottawa OTTAWA The forgotten aboriginals pf Labrador have spoken up to ensure that they are never forgotten again.The fnhu Nation, representing some I,400 Indians, filed a complaint yesterday with the Human Rights Commission of Canada. They allege that, since 1949, they have been treated inequitably by the federal government which they say, shirked .its constitutional responsibility for them as Indians. In making their case, the Innu have produced a brief with a w ealth of historical documents, including letters between then-Prime Minister Lester Pearson and then-Premier Joey Smallwood and federal cabinet memoranda and minutes. It's an overwhelming brief and demonstrates conclusively, I think, that the government of Canada violated the constitution by negotiating terms of union with Newfoundland in 1949 that left some I,000 aboriginal people Innu and Inuit entirely outside the agreement, as though the aboriginals -of Labrador were just ordinary citizens of their province and not Ottawa's responsibility. Oddly, it was an idealism of a sort that resulted in natives being ignored when Newfoundland became part of Canada. Historian Olive Dickason has demonstrated that a new attitude towards Indians became evident in Ottawa after World War II, one that repudiated the extreme domineering and restrictive mentality of the Indian Act. "World War II ushered in a change of attitude," Dickason writes in Canada's First Nations: A History of Founding Peoples from Earliest Times (McClelland & Stewart). "Amerindians, despite the fact they were not citizens, enlisted in proportionately higher numbers than did any other segment of the general population. . . . When they returned to civilian life, the restrictions and inequities of their lot on reserves became so glaringly evident that veterans' organizations and church groups mounted a campaign that resulted in the establishment of a joint Senate and House of Commons committee on the Indian Act, which' held hearings from 1946 to 1948." Phasing out Indian Act This was precisely the period when Canada and Newfoundland were about to negotiate the Terms of Union. Ottawa was now thinking of phasing out the Indian Act and gradually making of Indians just ordinary citizens in their respective provinces. The aboriginals of Labrador were the first recipients of the new thinking, when Canada refused to -take Labrador's natives under the aegis of the Indian Act and under Ottawa's administration. chunks.text: "Accessibility does not always necessarily exclude exclude intelligence," he explained. "Entertaining '.does not exclude thought." ; There are several Quebec movie directors better Known and more celebrated than George Mihalka. But more people pay to see Mihalka's movies. On Friday, his latest film, Bullet to Beijing, , opens at several theatres in town (the premiere was last night at the Imperial), a sequel to those great Len Deighton spy movies from the 1960s r starring Michael Caine as Harry Palmer, two of which - The Ipcress File and Funeral in Berlin-are arguably among the best films ever made in this genre. , Bullet to Beijing, shot in St. Petersburg and JiOndon, takes place in present-day Russia, in a : world where the Cold War is over and cold warriors warriors like Harry Palmer are out of official work -and forced to ply their craft as freelancers. I ' Caine reprises his role as Palmer, while my old . Mend Michael Sarrazin has a supporting role as , a washed-up CIA agent. The film also stars Jason Connery, son of Sean. Mihalka is a curious cross-cultural creature, an English-speaking Hungarian immigrant, one of 'Quebec's most prolific directors in film and TV (he did the first 19 episodes of Scoop), capable of making Canadian films that look American, and this time "a sort of black, tongue-in-cheek action thriller that looks British." His comedy La Florida was the top-grossing NICK AUF PER MAUR PAGE TWO COLUMN Canadian film two years ago, while his next one-L'Homme Ideal, due to open in September - will likely top it. The comedy features almost almost everybody in Quebec's entertainment industry His easy shift between cultures cultures is obviously a reflection of my old drinking buddy's background. His parents fled Hungary after the Soviet invasion in 1956, escaping through the countryside and taking refuge in France while George and a sister were left behind with grandparents. grandparents.His father, a fervent pacifist architect, spoke French but soon soured on France because of the Algerian troubles in the early '60s. He didn't want his son conscripted into the French army, so the parents came to Canada and sent for the children. "In those days, however," Mihalka explained, "it was hard to get architects' work if you could not speak English, so he ended up in construction work." The boy grew up on the South Shore, going to MacDonald-Cartier High School. Just before he turned 17, he applied for various summer jobs, including one at the Montreal Star. He was offered a job with "the publisher, which I assumed meant working in the printing plant." work, he was led into the office office of publisher J.G. Mc-Connell, Mc-Connell, the enormously wealthy, eccentric, hard-drinking hard-drinking and prolific art collector collector who owned what once was one of the most profitable profitable newspapers in Canada. The teenager's duties were vaguely defined "but it amounted to the best education education one could ever have had." "I'd arrive in the office at 8:30 in the

chunks.text: morning," he explained, explained, "and basically I'd read all the newspapers newspapers and periodicals that Mr. McConnell had coming coming in from all over the world - underground art magazines, political tracts, journals of every description. description. Basically I had to go through it all and clip out what interested him that week. One week it would be modern art, the next Asian economies, the next European fashion - he was very eclectic. "Then I'd do anything else he wanted me to do. Sometimes it would be to go to the Waddington art gallery to arrange a private showing by some artist that interested him and then I'd accompany him on his 'shopping trip.' He'd ask me if I liked a particular painting and if I said yes, he'd buy it. He bought dozens of objects at a time." Shortly after he joined the Star, the October Cri sis erupted and the elder Mihalka, pacifist worry- To his astonishment, when he showed up for wart, moved to Toronto while his son elected to stay on. The elder McConnell treated Mihalka as a "sort of protege, although he kept his family life strictly private." I knew McConnell's son at the time, and it was obvious father and son didn't get along all that well, the son being a bit hell-bent and mostly interested interested in cars. So it would seem to me in retrospect the old man might have viewed his Hungarian immigrant immigrant as a surrogate son. In any case, Mihalka got a nifty education in the 2 years he worked for him, not the least due to McConnell's habit of making all visitors wait at least 10 minutes in the outer office. Navy-blue pack on her back, brown recorder case in one hand, black schoolbag in the other, she's heavily laden but smiling: the day's classes are over. chunks.text: v p ' C6 THE GAZETTE, MONTREAL, FRIDAY, SEPTEMBER 3, 2004 FAST - WHERE ARE THEY NOW? IAN MacDONALD FORMULA ONE Schumi unhurt monza, italy - Formula One champion Michael Schumacher escaped uninjured yesterday after after a high-speed crash during a testing session. Schumacher's Ferrari was seriously damaged in the crash, which was attributed attributed to a problem with the back left tire. Medics attended to Schumacher after he climbed out of the car but he did not go to the track hospital for a precautionary precautionary exam, a Ferrari spokesperson said. The crash occurred at the end of the main straightaway, just before the Monza circuit's parabolic curve, in a portion of the track where cars reach their highest speeds. Ferrari was testing for the next Formula One race, the Sept. 12 Italian Grand Prix at Monza. Schumacher clinched his record seventh drivers' title - and fifth consecutive - on Sunday Sunday at the Belgian Grand Prix. NBA Barkley free Philadelphia - The woman who accused former basketball star Charles Barkley of groping her at a nightclub has withdrawn her police complaint. "It's a noncase. It's over with." her lawyer, A. Charles Peruto Jr., said, adding "everyone is under agreement that this was just a big misunderstanding. " The woman had told police the former former NBA star inappropriately touched her breast last week in a crowded nightclub. On Wednesday, Peruto said she was willing to drop any complaints, civil or criminal, as long as Barkley apologized. Peruto declined declined to say whether an apology apology occured, but said both sides were satisfied the issue was resolved. resolved. No money changed hands, he said. CFL Bombers sorry Winnipeg - The Winnipeg Blue Bombers apologized yesterday after criticism of a hazing incident incident by players. In a front-page story yesterday, the Winnipeg Free Press reported that Ian Heinl, a student athletic therapist therapist who was leaving the team, was grabbed by at least four players and bound to the goalpost goalpost with tape at the end of practice last week. OBITUARY ELEANOR ELLIS (nee Jones) Eleanor passed away peacefully September I at home with her family at her side, following a brief illness from lung cancer. She was born February 22, 1915 in Glovcrsville, New York and spent her early years there. She graduated from Smith College, Northampton, Masachusetts, and worked for several years in New York City before joining the American Red Cross. She served in Great Britain and Europe for two years during World War 11 and was awarded the Bronze Star and the Medal of Freedom. While stationed in Germany, she met Glenn Ellis, a Flight Lieutenant in the Royal Canadian Air Force. They were married in Gloversville on December 28, 1946 and she moved to Canada with him. In 1951, they moved to Town of Mt. Royal and began raising their two daughters. In 1961, they moved to Glens Falls, New York, later returning to Montreal. In 1968, they founded Sesame Industries LTD, a manufacturer and marketer of unique tapes for the packaging industry, located in St. Andre est, Quebec. Eleanor was Vice-president and Secretary -Treasurer of the Company. For twenty-one years they enjoyed a country home in nearby Carillon. In 1985, they sold the family business to H.B. Fuller Co. which continued to operate in St. Andre est until Fuller closed the factory in December 2003. Eleanor had an energetic zest for life, and a generous spirit. She was an active volunteer for many years for the Mayeourt Club in Montreal, the Unitarian Church in Montreal and Amnesty International, reflecting her passionate beliefs in human rights. Her thirst for knowledge and abundant curiosity made her an avid reader and lifelong lifelong learner and a regular attendant at courses, lectures, concerts and plays. From an early age, travel was one of Eleanor's chief delights and she visited doens of countries in her lifetime. Eleanor was a longtime subscriber to, and supporter of, several of Montreal's cultural institutions: the Montreal Symphony, the Centaur Theatre and Les Grands Ballets Canadiens. She was also an advocate for social environmental causes - writing letters for years on behalf of Amnesty International, supporting Greenpeace since it opened its doors and advocating recycling in her condominium. She is greatly missed by Glenn, their daughters Jacqueline of Portsmouth, New Hampshire and Antoinette (Toni) of Flora, Ontario and their five grandchildren: Lynn, Brian, Amie Vaccaro of Portsmouth and Joshua and Benjamin Taylor of Elora. The partners made a bold move back in 1976 when many in the jittery anglo community began the exodus along Highway 401 to Toronto and points beyond. Rather than joining the stampede, the two entrepreneurs staked a claim to a shopping mall on St. John's Blvd. in Pointe Claire, near the highway In the wake of the election of the Parti Quebecois government and its avowed goal of independence, it was an immense risk for Johnston and Scheunert. They plunked down their money and snapped up the strip mall, one of the earliest and one of the largest in Quebec when it was built in the 1950s, from the Steinberg family's Ivanhoe real-estate wing. The Steinberg's supermarket supermarket anchored the mall at the northwest corner. While the partners won't discuss numbers, it is safe to say they bought the mall for a rock-bottom price because because that's where real estate was in those days and where it languished for many years after. But in the face of political turbulence, turbulence, the revolution in retailing with the advent of the big-box stores, giant shopping centres, megacentres and fashion centres, Plaza Pointe Claire, as it is now known, has grown, innovated and grown some more. As new indoor malls were built, Scheunert and Johnston enclosed theirs and built space for more stores. As the population aged, they built a second storey to add offices for doctor's and medical labs. As homeowners began began cocooning, they built an expansion expansion on the southern end to house a garden centre. Bombardier Inc. chief executive executive Paul Tellier tried unsuccessfully last year to persuade chairperson Laurent Beaudoin to collapse the company's company's dual-class share structure into a one-share, one-vote setup. Tellier rightly saw abolition of the share structure as a stepping stone for Bombardier to obtain a listing on the New York Stock Exchange and access to a new audience of deep-pocketed U.S. investors. But the move was too much for Beaudoin and the Bombardier family to swallow. They control the company by virtue of Class A shares that carry 10 votes for every one vote carried by the Class B shares. The family couldn't face giving up control, so Bombardier remains remains off the BH( Board. Which brings us to the fall movie list, which gleams on the shelf with all its virgin promise, a litany of Oscar hopefuls, hopefuls, stories about people coming back from the dead, and movies featuring Jude Law and Angelina Jolie, who are unavoidable between now and Christmas. Christmas. Autumn is the best movie season: it's the time the studios haul out their quality products just in time for the Academy Award eligibility. Among the untarnished jewels are these dozen films of special interest. Sky Captain and the World of Tomorrow Finally, a chance to make a movie without all those annoying sets and locations. locations. In this adventure, newspaper reporter reporter Gwyneth Paltrow and ace aviator Jude Law investigate the disappearance of famous scientists around the world, while Angelina Jolie plays the commander commander of an all-female amphibious squadron. Her lips are only one of the movie's special effects: director Kerry Conran, who spent 10 years developing the project, filmed the whole thing against a blue screen, and every frame was digitally filled in later. Bottom line: Can it be more than acomputer-generated novelty? (Opens Sept. 17)

As its name implies, implies, the World Film Festival, which continues until Monday, screens movies from all over the globe. This year, the fest is showcasing 439 films from 72 countries, and Montrealers from, say, Brazil, or of Brazilian ancestry, ancestry, tend to turn up for the Brazilian flicks. People here with roots in other countries also often have a healthy curiosity curiosity for all kinds of world cinemas, which leads them to head to the fest for films from a variety of countries. Gail Charles and Claude Ango are emblematic of this type of fest-goer. Charles is a Montrealer with Trinida- dian Jamaican roots and her friend Ango moved here from Gabon in Africa five years ago. Charles is anglophone, anglophone, Ango is francophone, but the language difference doesn't stop them from sharing an enthusiasm for catching catching international cinema in a host of different languages at the festival. "I like seeing things other than American films to get a glimpse of other other cultures," said Charles. "I look for the type of films I won't have the chance to see otherwise. (This year) I want to see a Brazilian film because I've never seen a film from Brazil. I saw a documentary (The Color of Love) on how the concept of love is changing in Iran and I really liked it."
